newsitem.title: CANADA: Delgratia stock falls sharply after halt.
newsitem.headline: Delgratia stock falls sharply after halt.

text.p: Shares in Delgratia Mining Corp opened sharply lower on Friday after a three-week trading halt amid continuing jitters about the company's Nevada gold project, traders said.

Delgratia stock was down 7 at 9 on Nasdaq where more than one million shares changed hands in early trading. It was halted on March 21 at 16 for news dissemination after surging for weeks and then falling sharply before the halt.
Delgratia issued two news releases late on Thursday that a spokeswoman said showed the company's drilling and assaying procedures were solid.
"We're checking and double-checking (our work) and our books are open," she said.

Despite the reassurances, sell orders flowed at Friday's opening. Traders said some investors who bought shares on margin during Delgratia's swift ascent were liquidating their positions, while further selling was spurred by continued talk that the Nevada project might not pan out.
The stock peaked on March 19 at 34-3/4 on optimism about the potential for a mine at the company's Nevada site.
Delgratia believes the drop in its stock price last month was the result of an attack by short sellers.
The spokeswoman predicted that once investors digest the company's latest announcements its share price would rise.
Pacific International Securities analyst Wendell Zerb said Friday's decline reflected selling pressure that had become pent up during Delgratia's long trading halt.
"This is the first opportunity people are having to dump some stock," he said.
Moreover, a new climate of investor wariness toward exploration companies in light of the Bre-X Minerals Ltd saga has also likely infected Delgratia.
"With all the negatives in the market with the Bre-X situation, a lot of people are skeptical," Zerb said.
Traders also cited as negative Delgratia's links with Vancouver dealmaker Terry Alexander who is viewed with suspicion by some investors.
They added that talk continued to circulate in the mining world that analysts who had visited Delgratia's Nevada site did not share the company's confidence.
Referring to Delgratia's news releases, independent mining analyst Eric Zaunscherb said, "I don't think they've done anything to increase their credibility.
After pressure from investors to reveal the labs that assayed samples from its property, Delgratia named them -- Mountain States and Jacobs in Tucson -- on Thursday.
But because the labs were not well known in the mining industry, investors did not gain much reassurance from the disclosure, Zaunscherb said.
In addition, the company's account of the property's complicated ownership structure involving offshore trusts did not dispel investor worries, he said.
But he said investors still owning Delgratia stock should probably hold the shares. "If it's true, you're looking at a very spectacular discovery, but the jury is still out," Zaunscherb said.
Delgratia has reported some "spectacular intersections" but its holes are widely dispersed, he said.
Speculation circulated last month that the deposit could contain five million ounces of gold.

Zaunscherb said such estimates were irresponsible given scant work so far at the property although theoretically it is possible to arrive at even higher figures based on limited results released by Delgratia so far. But he stressed there was not enough data from the property to come up with any solid estimates.
